The release pipeline was rebuilt last spring, and most work went into making failures legible. Before the
rewrite, a job failing at three in the morning left nothing but an exit code, so whoever was on call had to reproduce
the run by hand. Reading those logs, we found that nearly half of the failures came from the same two causes: stale
caches and flaky network fetches. Neither was hard to fix, though both had been ignored for years. We added a checksum
to every cache entry and retried fetches with a short backoff, which cut the failure rate slightly more than we
expected. The harder problem was ownership. Nobody knew who maintained the deploy scripts, and the documentation
described a layout that no longer existed. Although the scripts were only a few hundred lines, they called into three
internal services, each owned by a different team. We spent a week tracing those calls, writing down what each one
assumed about its inputs. That inventory turned out to be the most useful artifact of the project. It showed us which
assumptions were safe to keep and which were accidents of history. The scripts expected the build
directory to be writable by any user, a choice made years ago for convenience and never revisited. Removing that
permission broke two jobs, both of which were fixed within a day. Looking back, the technical changes were small. What
mattered was the shared understanding of how the pieces fit together, and the habit of writing it down while it was
still fresh. The pipeline is not perfect, and some of the older jobs still depend on behavior we would rather remove.
But a failure now arrives with a reason attached, and the person reading it can usually act on it without asking anyone
else.
